summary: NBC News profiles NASA climate scientist Peter Kalmus, who copes with deep climate grief through meditation, civil disobedience, and a summer stay at the Possibility Alliance, an off-grid homestead in Belfast, Maine. Disillusioned with political leaders and the scientific community, he sought ways to withstand climate change rather than only stop it. He concluded that community and relationships, more than place, make survival and sanity possible.
one_line: NASA climate scientist Peter Kalmus, grieving and disillusioned, finds solace in community at the off-grid Possibility Alliance homestead in Maine.
key_facts: Peter Kalmus, 49, is a NASA climate scientist with about 340,000 followers on X who believes civilization is on a path to breakdown.
Kalmus meditates up to two hours a day to keep his climate anxiety at bay; otherwise, he says, "it's completely overwhelming."

About a decade ago Kalmus left a promising academic career in astrophysics to study the physics of climate change; he stopped flying, became a vegetarian and drives a Tesla, cutting his personal emissions by about 90% by his own math.

Kalmus has been arrested twice at climate protests, including chaining himself to a Chase bank in Los Angeles last year; NASA sent him a letter expressing concern, and he fears a third arrest could cost him his job.

In summer 2020 a California heat wave and nearby wildfire sickened him and killed a dogwood tree; a Pacific Northwest heat wave that year killed hundreds, leading him to realize "no place was safe." His family moved to North Carolina for his wife Sharon's work.

Kalmus criticizes President Joe Biden's Inflation Reduction Act as doing too little; Rhodium Group estimates emissions will fall 32%-42% below 2005 levels by 2030, with the bill responsible for about a quarter of the decrease.

He says the Paris Agreement will take the world to about 3 degrees Celsius of heating, and he doesn't think civilization would survive that; a 2022 UN report estimated 2.1 to 2.9 degrees Celsius by 2100.
A 2022 poll found almost two-thirds of Americans say they were affected by extreme weather; about 27% are "very worried" about climate change and one in 10 report anxiety or depression symptoms.

The Possibility Alliance is an 11-acre homestead in Belfast, Maine, run by the Hughes family, with no electricity, running water or sewer system; it uses a gift economy and plans to host climate refugees.

At the homestead Kalmus shared unpublished research on heat projections through 2300 and mourned the Amazon, which he said is probably past its tipping point; Timothy Lenton says the Amazon could cross a threshold at as little as 2 degrees C of warming.
In Belfast Kalmus played mandolin in a Celtic folk group, spoke at the local library and felt safer and more energized, realizing it was about the people, not the place.
Kalmus was planning a return trip to the Possibility Alliance over the winter holidays, saying "There's nothing more important in life than relationships."
